# Milestones of Space Exploration — provenance report

<!-- Generated from authored/space-exploration.json by scripts/authored_decks.py. Do not edit: change the dossier and rebuild. -->

**Deck:** [`decks/space-exploration.ttl`](../decks/space-exploration.ttl) · **Cards:** 48 · **Licence:** [CC0 1.0 Universal](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/) · **Compiled by:** Anton Wiklund · **Created:** 2026-10-04

48 milestones of space exploration, from Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite (1957), to Artemis II, the first crewed flight of the Artemis programme (2026), as of 4 October 2026. Front: the milestone, almost always an undisputed first, with the mission that achieved it, e.g. "First crewed landing on the Moon (Apollo 11)"; back: the year of the event itself (for a flyby or landing, not the launch year, which a note gives when it differs). Taken from Wikidata and NASA and checked against the Swedish Wikipedia.

## Licensing

The content sources are Wikidata (CC0) and NASA's websites (nasa.gov and science.nasa.gov: NASA content is generally not subject to copyright in the United States, and US government works are not protected, 17 U.S.C. § 105), so the deck is CC0 1.0. The milestones' facts and years and the English and Swedish names on the cards come from these two sources (the Swedish names are Wikidata sv labels or aliases, except the short form Apollo–Sojuz); the selection is the compiler's own (method step 1); the fronts and notes are the compiler's own wording and no NASA text was copied. The Swedish Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0), ESO's press release (CC BY 4.0, used for verification only so that the deck stays CC0), Xinhua's report as republished by the Chinese Academy of Sciences (all rights reserved) and the Astronomy Picture of the Day explanations (written by its editors; their licence was not established, so treated as all rights reserved) were used for verification only: they confirmed facts the content sources gave, and no wording or selection was taken from them. For one card, Chang'e 6, the word "first" is stated only by a verification source (Xinhua); NASA's Lunar Surface Data Book gives the facts it rests on (the return of the far-side samples on 25 June 2024, and Chang'e 4 in 2019 as the first landing on the far side). Facts are not copyrightable, so this does not affect the licence. NASA's list of robotic firsts, compiled from Siddiqi's "Beyond Earth", was used for dates and for which mission was first; the deck's selection, which mixes crewed and robotic milestones and leaves most of that list out, is the compiler's own. ESA's website, whose terms reserve all rights, was not used.

## Method

1. Who did the work: Anton Wiklund compiled this deck with the help of AI agents (Claude, by Anthropic), which did the research, drafting and cross-checking at his direction. The cards were checked by machine (live Wikidata and the app's SHACL and DCAT-AP validators) and in independent review rounds by further Claude agents, each logged under Quality control with its findings and how they were resolved. Anton Wiklund reviews every deck in full before it is released.
2. 1. Candidate milestones: a list of about 65 well-known milestones of space exploration (the ones the library editor's brief named, plus further firsts in human spaceflight, lunar and planetary exploration) was drawn up from general knowledge and then narrowed to firsts whose definition is not disputed (see Selection). Each candidate's Wikidata item was found with the Wikidata search API (query 2, wbsearchentities, one request per name) and confirmed by its label and description.
3. 2. Wikidata (content): query 1 fetched for every candidate item the English and Swedish labels, the Swedish Wikipedia article title and the dated statements P619 (UTC date of spacecraft launch), P620 (time of spacecraft landing), P621, P580, P582, P585, P571, P576 and P569; query 3 fetched the dated P793 (significant event) statements (flybys, orbit insertions, landings, extravehicular activities, maiden flight, impact), which hold the date of most robotic milestones; query 4 fetched all English, Swedish and mul labels and aliases of the people and of the items whose names differ between the languages; query 5 the Mir space station item (Q48604) and the item for the first image of a black hole (Q63105182). Query 6 fetched the COSPAR identifiers (P247) used for step 3.
4. 3. NASA (content): the NSSDCA Master Catalog pages of the spacecraft (query 7, by COSPAR id) answered with an error page ("An error has occurred") for most non-US spacecraft and for Explorer 1, Hubble, Galileo, Zarya and Huygens on the day of research and were therefore not used as evidence; the NSSDCA "Chronology of Lunar and Planetary Exploration" (query 8) lists launches only. The NASA pages used instead (queries 11–15, fetched with <scratch>/fetch_pages.py, which saves each page's HTML and its plain text with tags, scripts and styles removed) are the mission pages of nasa.gov and science.nasa.gov, NASA History articles, the NSSDCA "Soviet Missions to the Moon" page and NASA Science's "Deep Space Robotic Firsts" list, a NASA Science resource page and the NASA Technical Publication "Lunar Surface Data Book" (query 22) (https://science.nasa.gov/deep-space-exploration/, compiled from Asif Siddiqi's "Beyond Earth", NASA History Program Office, 2018). The sentence or table row that states the milestone and its date was extracted from each page's text with <scratch>/greps2.py and <scratch>/greps.sh (query 16; both split the saved text into sentences and print those matching a regular expression, greps.sh by calling <scratch>/grep.py) and is quoted in the card's evidence.
5. 4. Recent milestones: Artemis II was checked against live sources on the day of research (web search, query 17, and the NASA mission page): it launched on 1 April 2026 and splashed down on 10 April 2026 (local time; 11 April UTC in Wikidata and the Swedish Wikipedia), so it is in the deck. The 2024 milestones (Chang'e 6, Polaris Dawn) were confirmed from NASA pages, Wikidata and, for Chang'e 6, Xinhua's report of 25 June 2024 as republished by the Chinese Academy of Sciences. Nothing planned but not yet flown on 4 October 2026 is included.
6. 5. Independent check and Swedish: the introductions (query 9) and, where needed, full texts (query 10) of the Swedish Wikipedia articles on every mission and person were fetched through the MediaWiki API with their revision ids; each card's year, the milestone and the Swedish names were compared with them by reading. Swedish names follow the Wikidata sv labels, which equal the Swedish Wikipedia article titles apart from disambiguation such as "Zarja (ISS)" (Jurij Gagarin, Valentina Teresjkova, Aleksej Leonov, Svetlana Savitskaja, Lajka, Voschod 2, Saljut 1, Lunochod 1, Zarja, Sojuz T-12, James Webb-teleskopet); two cards use an sv alias instead, so that one form is used throughout: "Hubbleteleskopet" (the article title; the sv label is "Rymdteleskopet Hubble"), in the style of "James Webb-teleskopet", and "Bruce McCandless II" (the sv label is "Bruce McCandless"), the same form as in English. The front of the Apollo–Soyuz card uses the short form "Apollo–Sojuz" rather than the label "Apollo-Sojuz-testprojektet"; the Swedish fronts use the terms of those articles (rymdpromenad, förbiflygning, omloppsbana, rymdstation, månens baksida, rymdfärja). Two further checks are verification only: ESO's press release eso1907 for the first image of a black hole, and Xinhua's report on Chang'e 6 as republished by the Chinese Academy of Sciences. Two APOD explanations (Luna 9, Chang'e 4) were read as verification only.
7. 6. Cards: the front names the milestone in the compiler's own words, in English and Swedish, with the mission (and for crewed firsts the person) that achieved it, e.g. "First crewed landing on the Moon (Apollo 11)"; the back is the year in which the milestone itself happened (text in no language, zxx): for a flyby, orbit insertion or landing that is the year of the encounter, not of the launch. Where the launch was in an earlier year, a back note gives the launch year ("Launched in 1972."), to keep the two apart; a few other notes give context (Artemis II's dates, the 2017 observations behind the black-hole image, when Voyager 1's crossing was announced). Dates in different time zones (Explorer 1: 31 January local time, 1 February UTC; Galileo: 7/8 December; Voyager 2 at Neptune: 24/25 August; Luna 2: 13 September UT, 14 September Moscow time; Artemis II's splashdown: 10/11 April) never change the year. Study direction front to back only, because several milestones share a year.
8. 7. Machine checks: for every card whose year is a Wikidata statement of the event itself (the launch of a crewed flight, a station or a telescope; a landing, P620; the start of Expedition 1 and Apollo–Soyuz, P580; the publication of the black-hole image, P577) the builder checks that year against live Wikidata, and it checks the launch year given in a back note (P619), as well as the launch year (P619) of the robotic cards whose launch was in the same year as the milestone and the English and Swedish names of people and transliterated missions (labels or aliases). The dates of flybys, orbit insertions and other P793 events are qualifiers, which the builder cannot reach; they rest on query 3 and the NASA and Swedish Wikipedia evidence. The built deck was validated with the app's SHACL and DCAT-AP validators (validate_sources.ts).
9. 8. Helper scripts (in the scratch directory, not published; the rules here are what they do): search.py sends one wbsearchentities request per candidate name (query 2); nssdca.py fetches the NSSDCA Master Catalog page of each COSPAR id (query 7); svwiki.py fetches the introductions and current revision ids of the Swedish Wikipedia articles in batches of 15 (query 9); svfull.py fetches the full plain text of the named articles and prints the sentences matching the given regular expression (query 10); fetch_pages.py, grep.py, greps2.py and greps.sh are described in step 3. The query numbers in card evidence refer to the list of queries; the COSPAR query is number 6 although its files are named q2.rq/q2.csv, after the order in which they were written.

## Selection

48 milestones of space exploration from 1957 to 2026, as of 4 October 2026, each a first (or, for the Voyager probes, Mir, Zarya, Hubble and the James Webb Space Telescope, a launch) whose definition is not disputed and whose year all sources agree on. Included: the first satellites (Sputnik 1, Sputnik 2 with Laika, the first US satellite), the firsts of crewed spaceflight (first human, woman, spacewalk, untethered spacewalk, spacewalk by a woman, docking, lunar orbit, Moon landing, space station, international docking, orbital Space Shuttle flight, ISS resident crew, China's first crewed flight, first commercial spacewalk, the first crewed Artemis flight), the firsts of robotic exploration of the Moon, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Neptune, Pluto, Titan, an asteroid and a comet, Voyager 1's entry into interstellar space, the first flight on another planet, the first asteroid-deflection test and the first image of a black hole (a ground-based observation, included because the library editor's brief asked for it). Left out because the definition of the first is disputed or the sources disagree: the first landing on Mars (Mars 3 in 1971, which fell silent after seconds, or Viking 1 in 1976), the first soft landing on the Moon (NASA's list of firsts gives Luna 9 a "survivable landing" and Surveyor 1 the first "soft-landing"; the Luna 9 card is therefore about the first photographs from the surface), the first commercial Moon landing, the first space tourist and the first landing of an orbital rocket booster. Left out to keep the deck near the requested size: other national firsts (the first American woman in space, the first US space station), the first flyby of Uranus, the first orbiters of the Moon, Saturn and Mercury, the first asteroid sample return and further missions. The Huygens card is limited to what the sources state (the first landing on Titan); the wider claim that it was the first landing on any moon other than ours was found only in the English Wikipedia and is not on the card.

  } UNION {
    <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MESSENGER> schema:about ?item .

## Quality control

5 rounds, 33 findings: 24 fixed, 0 rejected after checking, 9 needing no change. Every card's Wikidata checks (75 in all) are re-run against live Wikidata by `scripts/authored_decks.py check` before every build.

### Round 0: Sources, licences and machine checks: every card's milestone and year against Wikidata, NASA and the Swedish Wikipedia (and ESO, the Chinese Academy of Sciences and APOD where named); recency of the 2024–2026 milestones; the definitions of the firsts; the Swedish names against Wikidata sv labels and the Swedish Wikipedia. (2026-10-04)

**Reviewer:** Claude (AI) — authoring agent, machine checks · **Scope:** All 48 cards, the sources and the deck metadata.

Wikidata, NASA and the Swedish Wikipedia agree on the year of every milestone on the cards. The disagreements found are in exact dates (time zones, typing errors on NASA pages), in one Wikidata launch date and in which mission some NASA pages credit with a first; none changes a year on a card. Candidate firsts whose definition the sources dispute were left out or reworded. One Wikidata check was not added because Wikidata's value is wrong (Pioneer 10's launch date); no other check was skipped.

| Card | Issue | Resolution | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| pioneer-10 | Wikidata's P619 for Pioneer 10 is 1973-03-03, but its own P793 rocket-launch statement, NASA (launch in March 1972) and the Swedish Wikipedia ("2 mars 1972") give 1972; the P619 value looks like a typing error of the year. | The note says "Launched in 1972." and has no Wikidata check (a check against P619 would fail, and the card's year 1973 must not be checked against the wrong launch date either). Recorded in the card's evidence. | fixed |
| venera-9 | NASA's "Deep Space Robotic Firsts" list gives "First spacecraft to transmit photos from the surface of another planet: USSR / Venera 10 / 22 October 1975", but 22 October 1975 is Venera 9's landing (Wikidata P620; Venera 10 landed three days later); NASA's "First Look: Venus" page, NASA's Venus mission table ("Venera 9 … Success-First") and the Swedish Wikipedia credit Venera 9. | The card names Venera 9, as most sources do; the year (1975) is the same for both landers. | no change needed |
| luna-9 | Whether Luna 9 made the first soft landing on the Moon is disputed: NASA's Moon page and APOD say it did, NASA's list of firsts (after Siddiqi) calls it the first "survivable landing" and gives the first "soft-landing" to Surveyor 1 (June 1966). | The card asks for the first photographs from the Moon's surface, which all sources credit to Luna 9 (February 1966). | fixed |
| huygens | The claim that Huygens made the first landing on a moon other than Earth's, or the first in the outer Solar System, was found only in the English Wikipedia, not in the sources used. | The front says only what NASA states: the first landing on Titan. | fixed |
| mariner-4 | NASA's Mariner 4 page gives the flyby as "July 14, 1965" in its facts and "June 14, 1965" in a timeline entry, and NASA's list of firsts has "Launched 15 July 1965" (the launch was on 28 November 1964); Wikidata has the flyby on 1965-07-15 (UTC). | Typing errors on the NASA pages; the flyby year 1965 is the same in every source. The note gives the launch year 1964 (Wikidata P619, checked). | no change needed |
| near-shoemaker | NASA's list of firsts gives the landing on Eros as 12 February 2001 in one section and 13 February 2001 in another. | Wikidata and the other sources give 12 February 2001; the year is the same. | no change needed |
| luna-2 | The impact is 13 September 1959 in NASA's history article (21:02 UT) and the Swedish Wikipedia, 14 September in Wikidata and NASA's list of firsts (Moscow time). | Time zones; the year is the same. | no change needed |
| artemis-2 | A 2026 milestone: whether Artemis II had flown by 4 October 2026 had to be confirmed from live sources. | NASA's mission page ("LaunchED April 1, 2026 splashdown April 10, 2026"), Wikidata (P619 2026-04-01, P620 2026-04-11 UTC) and the Swedish Wikipedia agree that it flew; the card is included with a note on its dates. | no change needed |
| voskhod-2 | Wikidata's English label is "Alexey Leonov"; NASA writes "Aleksei A. Leonov" and many English texts "Alexei Leonov". | The English front uses the Wikidata label "Alexey Leonov" (checked by the builder); the Swedish front the sv label "Aleksej Leonov", the title of the Swedish article. | no change needed |
| hubble-launch | Wikidata's Swedish label of Hubble is "Rymdteleskopet Hubble", the Swedish Wikipedia's article title "Hubbleteleskopet" (an sv alias). | The Swedish front writes "rymdteleskopet Hubble" in running text; the year is checked on P619 rather than on the label. | no change needed |
| shenzhou-5 | No NASA page on Shenzhou 5 could be read: its NSSDCA catalogue page and a 2005 NASA report page gave errors. | The card rests on Wikidata (content) and two Swedish Wikipedia articles, which agree (15 October 2003). | no change needed |
| sputnik-1 | The NSSDCA Master Catalog answered with an error page for most spacecraft (all Soviet, Chinese and several US ones) on the day of research. | The catalogue was not used; NASA mission pages, NASA History articles and NASA Science's list of firsts were used instead (method step 3). | no change needed |

### Round 1: Factual accuracy (2026-10-04)

**Reviewer:** Claude (AI) — independent Factual accuracy reviewer · **Scope:** All 48 cards; 9 re-checked against live Wikidata, the rest against established mission dates.

Every year on a back is correct. Two cards lacked the launch-year note that the description promises, one front was ambiguous, and two suggestions concerned a note and missing Wikidata year checks. All were verified against live Wikidata (query 24) and applied, except a year check on Pioneer 10, whose Wikidata launch date is wrong.

| Card | Issue | Resolution | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| sojourner | The back is the landing year 1997, but Mars Pathfinder was launched in 1996 and the card had no launch-year note, which the description promises. | Confirmed: Wikidata Q201771 P619 1996-12-04, P620 1997-07-04. Added the note "Launched in 1996." / "Uppskjuten 1996." and a check of Q201771 P619 = 1996. | fixed |
| change-4 | The back is the landing year 2019, but Chang'e 4 was launched in 2018 and the card had no launch-year note. | Confirmed: Wikidata Q723045 P619 2018-12-07, P620 2019-01-03. Added the note "Launched in 2018." / "Uppskjuten 2018." and a check of Q723045 P619 = 2018. | fixed |
| sts-1 | "First Space Shuttle flight" could also be read as Enterprise's free flights in the 1977 Approach and Landing Tests. | Front reworded to "First orbital flight of the Space Shuttle (STS-1, Columbia)" / "Rymdfärjans första färd i omloppsbana (STS-1, Columbia)", as Wikidata describes STS-1 ("first orbital flight of the Shuttle Columbia"); the selection text now says "orbital Space Shuttle flight". | fixed |
| artemis-2 | The note says 1–10 April 2026, while Wikidata's P620 is 2026-04-11 (UTC). | Both are right (the splashdown was on the evening of 10 April US time). The note now says "(US time)" / "(amerikansk tid)" and the evidence explains the difference. Live Wikidata now also has a second P619 value, 2026-02-15, that no other source gives as the launch date; it is in 2026, so the card's check still holds, and the evidence records it. | fixed |
| lunokhod-1 | No check on the year, although Wikidata has a launch date in the same year; the same applies to mariner-2, mariner-9, pioneer-10, luna-3 and change-6. | Added P619 checks where the launch year equals the milestone year: lunokhod-1 (Q261052, 1970), mariner-2 (Q208984, 1962), mariner-9 (Q203801, 1971), luna-3 (Q942814, 1959) and change-6 (Q18346001, 2024). Not for pioneer-10: its Wikidata P619 is 1973-03-03, a wrong launch date (round 0; the launch was in March 1972), and checking the card's year 1973 against it would pass only by that error. | fixed |

### Round 2: Language, translation and language tags (2026-10-04)

**Reviewer:** Claude (AI) — independent Language, translation and language tags reviewer · **Scope:** All 48 cards in the dossier and the built deck, plus the title, description and keywords.

Language tags, study direction, description length and keywords are correct. Three warnings on Swedish wording (inconsistent telescope names, an unidiomatic verb, a calque in the description) and two suggestions on Swedish phrasing and a name form; all were applied.

| Card | Issue | Resolution | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| hubble-launch | The Swedish names of the two telescopes follow different styles: "rymdteleskopet Hubble" but "James Webb-teleskopet". | Confirmed in live Wikidata (query 24): Q2513 has the sv alias "Hubbleteleskopet", which is also the Swedish Wikipedia title. The Swedish front is now "Uppskjutningen av Hubbleteleskopet (STS-31)", with a label/alias check; method step 5 explains the choice.
